topic.title: Amino acids, peptides, proteins
topic.publicationChapter: Understanding Peptides — Two: Amino acids, peptides, proteins
topic.summary: Amino acids share a common backbone and differ by their side chains; twenty make up the standard set; the sequence is the primary structure, and it carries the information for folding into secondary and tertiary structure.
topic.notes: What else changes as a chain gets longer — stability, immune recognition — is not stated by any permissive source held.

claims.claimText: A 2022 Essays in Biochemistry review defines secondary structure as regular, recurring elements (alpha-helices and beta-sheets) formed by interactions between atoms of the peptide backbone - the chain excluding the variable side chains.
claims.plainLanguageText: The backbone is the repeating spine of the chain, without the side chains that hang off it. Stretches of backbone can coil into helices or line up into sheets.
claims.interpretationNotes: Supplies a backbone definition (ch1 b) and the secondary-structure level (ch2 b).
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review. General biochemistry, not about any peptide product.

evidence.interpretation: Supplies a backbone definition (ch1 b) and the secondary-structure level (ch2 b).
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: A 2023 review in Life states that each genetically encoded amino acid has a constant backbone - an amine at one end, a carboxyl at the other and an alpha carbon between them - and that the variable side chain on that carbon distinguishes one amino acid from another.
claims.plainLanguageText: Every amino acid shares the same core: an amino group, an acid group and a central carbon. What makes each one different is the side chain attached to that carbon.
claims.interpretationNotes: Box 1 text within the Introduction; '(A)', '(B)' refer to figure panels.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review. General biochemistry, not about any peptide product.

evidence.interpretation: Box 1 text within the Introduction; '(A)', '(B)' refer to figure panels.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: The same review describes the genetically encoded set of 20 amino acids, often called the canonical set, as an 'alphabet' established early in biological evolution.
claims.plainLanguageText: Living things build proteins from a standard 'alphabet' of 20 amino acids.
claims.interpretationNotes: Evolutionary-history clause is the authors' interpretation; the alphabet framing can be used without it.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review. General biochemistry, not about any peptide product.

evidence.interpretation: Evolutionary-history clause is the authors' interpretation; the alphabet framing can be used without it.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: A 2020 review in Antibiotics states that an amino acid's side chain determines whether it is hydrophilic or hydrophobic and whether it exists as a charged or neutral molecule.
claims.plainLanguageText: The side chain gives each amino acid its character - for example, whether it mixes with water or avoids it, and whether it carries an electric charge.
claims.interpretationNotes: Charge also depends on pH (not stated in this quote - do not add without a source).
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review. General biochemistry, not about any peptide product.

evidence.interpretation: Charge also depends on pH (not stated in this quote - do not add without a source).
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A review. The primary studies it cites have not been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: The 2022 Essays in Biochemistry review defines primary structure as the amino acid sequence making up a protein's polypeptide chain.
claims.plainLanguageText: The order of amino acids along the chain is called the primary structure.
claims.interpretationNotes: A definitional statement, taken as the source states it.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review. General biochemistry, not about any peptide product.

evidence.interpretation: A definitional statement, taken as the source states it.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: The same review defines tertiary structure as the overall structure of the whole protein, mediated mainly by interactions between amino acid side chains - including hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, van der Waals interactions, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions that induce folding.
claims.plainLanguageText: The complete folded shape of a protein is its tertiary structure. It is held together mostly by different kinds of contacts between side chains.
claims.interpretationNotes: The quaternary-structure sentence that follows was left out to keep the quote under 60 words; the brief only covers primary to tertiary structure.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review. General biochemistry, not about any peptide product.

evidence.interpretation: The quaternary-structure sentence that follows was left out to keep the quote under 60 words; the brief only covers primary to tertiary structure.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: A 2016 Biochemical Journal review states that, as Anfinsen proposed, the way proteins fold into their functional structures is dictated by information encoded in their amino acid sequence.
claims.plainLanguageText: The order of amino acids carries the instructions for how a protein folds into its working shape.
claims.interpretationNotes: Secondary attribution to Anfinsen. Cellular folding can involve helper proteins - not covered here; avoid 'always folds on its own'.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review. General biochemistry, not about any peptide product.

evidence.interpretation: Secondary attribution to Anfinsen. Cellular folding can involve helper proteins - not covered here; avoid 'always folds on its own'.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A review. The primary studies it cites have not been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: The same review states that one key event in folding is the collapse of the unfolded chain so that hydrophobic side chains are excluded from the surrounding solvent.
claims.plainLanguageText: Part of folding is the chain curling up so that its water-avoiding side chains are tucked away from the surrounding water.
claims.interpretationNotes: 'One of the key events', not the whole mechanism.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review. General biochemistry, not about any peptide product.

evidence.interpretation: 'One of the key events', not the whole mechanism.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: Brown et al. (2023) state that, since the genetically encoded set of 20 amino acids was established, the greatest deviations have been the addition of a 21st amino acid, selenocysteine, within some lineages of bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes, and a 22nd, pyrrolysine, in archaea and bacteria.
claims.plainLanguageText: Some living things use one or two amino acids beyond the standard 20.
claims.interpretationNotes: Introduction, paragraph 2, the same paragraph as FND-10. The source does not say which organisms use selenocysteine, including whether humans do; do not add it. The evolutionary time-scale framing is the authors' and is not carried.
claims.uncertaintyText: Foundational statement from a peer-reviewed review. General biochemistry, not about any peptide product.

evidence.interpretation: Amino acids beyond the canonical twenty.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A review. The primary studies it cites have not been obtained and read by this index.
